name: Vocal cord filler injection

lead: Vocal cord filler injection, medically called injection laryngoplasty, places material into a vocal fold to add bulk and move it toward the midline so the folds meet better, giving a fuller, stronger voice. Appearance-focused communities discuss it as a way to restore voice volume.

Materials listed include autologous fat, collagen, hyaluronates and hydroxyapatite. Registered trials have examined silk-protein filler, platelet-rich fibrin with fat, and injection for voice tremor, all in patients with medical voice conditions such as paralysis or weakness. No cosmetic-use studies in healthy people were reviewed.

paras: It is performed by a laryngologist as a medical procedure, with the material chosen for the patient. Temporary materials wear off over roughly 2 to 12 months, so results can be repeated or made longer-lasting with other materials.
Temporary materials wear off, and techniques are not standardised. Specific complications are not detailed in the sources reviewed; it is a procedure for medical voice conditions.

angle.text: Injection laryngoplasty adds bulk to a vocal fold so the folds meet better, giving a fuller, stronger voice. It is discussed in appearance communities, while the research comes from medical use in vocal fold paralysis, weakness and tremor.

lead: Vocal cord filler injection, medically called injection laryngoplasty or injection augmentation, places material into a vocal fold to add bulk and move it toward the midline so the two folds meet better when a person speaks. In clinical practice it is used for vocal fold paralysis and weakness, where a gap between the folds makes the voice rough, breathy or tiring.[1][2]

Appearance-focused communities discuss it under voice improvement: the effect people look for is a fuller, stronger-sounding voice with better projection. Wikipedia describes the symptoms it addresses as a rough or breathy voice, vocal fatigue, reduced stamina, a narrower pitch range and trouble projecting over noise.[1][2]

Materials listed include autologous fat, collagen, hyaluronates, hydroxyapatite, Teflon, acellular dermis and fascia; effects of temporary materials last roughly 2 to 12 months.[1] Registered trials have examined silk-protein filler, platelet-rich fibrin with fat, and injection for voice tremor, all in patients with medical voice conditions.[3][4][5]

paras: Wikipedia reports that vocal fold paresis is injury to the recurrent laryngeal nerve, with causes including surgery such as thyroidectomy, intubation, tumors, infections and neurologic disease. Observation comes first for possible spontaneous recovery, then voice therapy with a speech-language pathologist, and if paralysis has not resolved after about 9 months and voice therapy is unsatisfactory, temporary injection medialization is the next option.[1] Neither technique nor materials are standardised across clinicians.[1][2]

For significant paralysis at about 12 months, medialization thyroplasty places an implant to support the fold in a more central position, and arytenoid adduction or laryngeal reinnervation are further options.[1] The article notes that surgical options generally improve voice, but none has been shown to be clearly superior to the others.[1]

One-sided nerve damage most often causes a rough or breathy voice, vocal fatigue and reduced stamina, and patients may also have a narrower pitch range and trouble projecting in noise.[1][2] Clinicians combine history, perceptual voice rating, endoscopy and stroboscopy to assess movement.[1]

Trials registered on ClinicalTrials.gov include a completed 11-patient study of silk protein microparticle filler for vocal cord paralysis and dysphonia (started 2020),[3] a 19-patient phase 4 study adding platelet-rich fibrin to autologous fat for vocal cord paralysis (started 2018),[4] and an 8-patient study of botulinum toxin and injection augmentation for essential voice tremor (started 2015).[5] Results are not summarised in the registrations. No studies were found of the procedure for cosmetic voice change in people without a voice disorder.

The Wikipedia article reports that injection results vary in duration and that techniques are not standardised; it does not give a detailed list of procedure-specific complications.[1] Bilateral paralysis carries airway-obstruction risk as a condition.[1]
The procedure is mentioned in discussion of voice improvement among surgical options. No community material is available to attribute in detail.
